paragraphs: A sentence can support more than one grammatical structure or interpretation. This paper investigates language comprehension through a model that treats readers as Bayesian reasoners. In that framework, competing interpretations have probabilities, giving the model a way to express preferences among possible readings rather than merely selecting a grammatical analysis.

The authors extend an earlier account that represented comprehension using Bayesian decision trees. Their contribution is to make further predictions about reading time from the probabilities of different parses or interpretations. This connects two aspects of comprehension: which interpretation a reader favors and how long processing takes. Reading time therefore becomes an observable quantity against which the probabilistic account can be checked.

The extended model is tested against reading-time measurements from a psycholinguistic experiment. The supplied abstract establishes this link between probabilistic interpretation and experimental testing, without specifying the outcome of the comparison. The contribution is a more directly testable account of comprehension, connecting uncertainty about sentence meaning with the timing of human reading.
neurips-2001-a-bayesian-model-predicts-h.tldr: An extended Bayesian model links the probabilities of sentence interpretations to reading-time predictions tested against human data.

paragraphs: Principal component analysis reduces the dimensionality of data while implicitly measuring reconstruction errors with squared loss. This paper questions whether that measurement is appropriate for every kind of observation. Binary data provide the motivating example: a representation designed around real-valued errors may not reflect the structure of observations that take only two values.

The authors generalize PCA by drawing together ideas from exponential-family distributions, generalized linear models, and Bregman distances. These ingredients provide a route to alternative loss functions while retaining the goal of dimensionality reduction. The central change is therefore in what counts as a good approximation to the data, allowing that choice to reflect the data type.

The paper also describes algorithms for minimizing the resulting losses and illustrates the approach with simulated data. Its contribution combines a broader formulation with methods for fitting it. The authors argue that the alternative losses are better suited to other observation types; the abstract does not establish that one generalized version is best for all data.
neurips-2001-a-generalization-of-princip.tldr: The paper generalizes PCA to alternative loss functions intended to better match data types such as binary observations.

paragraphs: Multisensory enhancement occurs when input through one sense strengthens a neuron's response to input through another. The paper models this phenomenon while also addressing the decisions an observer must make about a stimulus. In particular, the model needs to handle visual and auditory signals that do not agree.

The proposed maximum-likelihood model modifies an earlier Bayesian account by introducing a decision strategy aimed at maximizing correct decisions. This addition lets the model address stimulus discrimination and identification under incongruent sensory cues. The approach connects the size of a neural response with the broader problem of using multiple sources of sensory evidence to decide what is present.

The model accounts for inverse effectiveness reported in neural recordings, where enhancement is related to the effectiveness of the individual sensory inputs. It also predicts a functional relationship between discriminability with one modality and with two. That relationship is presented as testable through both neural recordings and behavioral experiments, giving the model a prediction beyond its account of an existing response pattern.
neurips-2001-a-maximum-likelihood-approa.tldr: A maximum-likelihood model connects multisensory enhancement with stimulus decisions and predicts a testable relationship between single-sense and combined-sense discrimination.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to recover separate sources from observed signals that are instantaneous linear mixtures. The mixing matrix is unknown, so the method must work without being told how the sources were combined. Its starting point is that separation can improve when sources have sparse representations in an appropriate collection of signal features.

The authors use multiscale transforms, including wavelets and wavelet packets, to break signals into local features. Different subsets of those features have different degrees of sparsity. The algorithm exploits this variation by choosing the sparsest subsets for subsequent separation. Feature selection is therefore tied to where the transformed signals offer the strongest sparse structure.

The approach is evaluated on both noisy and noise-free data, with experiments covering simulated signals, musical sounds, and images. The authors report substantial improvements in separation quality over previously reported results. These findings support selecting informative parts of a multiscale representation for the tested separation problems, while the stated problem formulation remains unknown instantaneous linear mixing.
neurips-2001-blind-source-separation-via.tldr: Selecting the sparsest subsets of multiscale signal features improves blind source separation in experiments with signals, music, and images.

paragraphs: Some biological neurons change their connection strengths according to the precise timing difference between incoming and outgoing spikes. This observation motivates learning rules in which the temporal relationship between spikes matters. The paper investigates how such temporally asymmetric Hebbian rules can be implemented in analog silicon circuitry.

The authors argue that these rules are suitable for analog VLSI and describe a circuit that changes the weight of a silicon spiking neuron accordingly. A central design feature is that the circuit is easily tunable. This makes the work a concrete hardware treatment of timing-dependent learning, connecting a proposed rule for synaptic modification with a circuit that can implement it.

The circuit was fabricated using a 0.6-micrometer CMOS process, and the paper presents test results from that fabrication. Its contribution therefore extends beyond proposing a learning rule or outlining an implementation. It supplies a built circuit and experimental tests, supporting investigation of how biologically motivated changes in connection strength can be realized in silicon.
neurips-2001-citcuits-for-vlsi-implement.tldr: The paper presents and tests a tunable analog circuit that implements spike-timing-dependent changes to a silicon neuron's weight.

paragraphs: Mutual information measures statistical dependence between variables, but a value calculated from observed frequencies is only a point estimate. It does not by itself express uncertainty about the underlying dependence. This paper asks how to assess questions such as whether an estimate is compatible with zero or whether the true value could be substantially larger.

The authors use a Bayesian treatment of the unknown joint probabilities. A prior over those probabilities is updated using observed counts, producing a posterior. That posterior then induces a distribution over mutual information. The resulting object describes uncertainty about dependence itself, rather than reporting just the dependence measured in the sample.

The paper derives approximations described as reliable and quick to compute, focusing on the distribution's mean, variance, skewness, and kurtosis with non-informative priors. It also provides an exact expression for the mean and discusses numerical behavior and validity ranges. These results make uncertainty-aware use of mutual information more accessible, including in applications such as learning Bayesian networks.
neurips-2001-distribution-of-mutual-info.tldr: A Bayesian analysis provides efficient approximations to the uncertainty distribution of mutual information, including an exact expression for its mean.

paragraphs: Support vector regression uses an epsilon-tube to express a band of tolerated prediction error. This paper develops a geometric account of when such tubes exist. The authors show that the regression problem can be understood as a classification problem in a dual space, connecting the construction of a regression band to the separation of geometric sets.

The construction shifts the training responses upward and downward by epsilon, producing two versions of the data. Hard tubes correspond to separating their convex hulls, while soft tubes use reduced convex hulls. This gives a geometric interpretation to both forms of the regression problem and makes the role of the shifted responses explicit.

The authors then propose a new SVR model that chooses the maximum-margin plane between the shifted datasets. Increasing this margin corresponds to reducing the effective tube width. The stated benefit is interpretability: the effects of parameter choices become visible through the geometry, providing a unified way to understand the proposed model's behavior.
neurips-2001-duality-geometry-and-suppor.tldr: A geometric reformulation connects support vector regression to dual-space classification and motivates a maximum-margin regression model.

paragraphs: In multiple-instance learning, a label applies to a bag of instances, leaving uncertainty about which instance accounts for that label. EM-DD addresses this uncertainty by combining expectation-maximization with the diverse density algorithm. It is designed as a general-purpose method that accepts Boolean or real-valued labels and produces real-valued predictions.

The central move is to use EM to estimate the instance responsible for each bag's label. With that assignment estimated, the learning problem can be treated in a single-instance setting. This gives the method a broader conceptual role: it supplies a framework for translating bag-level supervision into a form that more directly identifies the examples driving the labels.

On the Boolean Musk benchmarks, the authors report that EM-DD significantly outperforms all previous algorithms without tuning. They also report relative insensitivity to the number of relevant attributes and good scaling to large bags. These findings support the method's practical value in the evaluated setting, alongside its stated ability to handle more than Boolean labels.
neurips-2001-em-dd-an-improved-multiple-.tldr: EM-DD estimates which instance explains a bag's label, combining EM and diverse density to improve multiple-instance learning.

paragraphs: Unsupervised methods such as independent component analysis can discover projections that separate observed data into components. A further question is whether those projections are reliable. This paper addresses that question by estimating uncertainty, aiming to provide information analogous to error bars and to assess the quality of the resulting separation.

The authors use resampling methods to estimate variance in the discovered projections. Experimentally, their variance estimates are strongly correlated with separation error. That relationship is useful because it connects an uncertainty measure to the quality of the separation, giving the reliability estimate a practical interpretation beyond simply describing variation across resampled data.

The paper demonstrates uses of reliability estimation for choosing an ICA model, substantially improving separation performance, and identifying components with physical meaning. An application to 49-channel magnetoencephalography data illustrates its usefulness on a neural recording problem. The contribution is thus both an uncertainty estimate and a demonstration that the estimate can guide model selection and interpretation of extracted components.
neurips-2001-estimating-the-reliability-.tldr: Resampling-based reliability estimates correlate with ICA separation error and help select models and identify meaningful components.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the computational cost of estimating hyperparameters in large networks. Its goal is to obtain useful estimates quickly while maintaining precision. The proposed approach uses information about a network's response, bringing together a theoretical response relation and an empirical measurement as the basis for parameter estimation.

Specifically, the method draws on the linear-response relation from the cavity method and measures a Green's function empirically. The Green's function supplies response information used by the estimation procedure. The important connection is between that measured behavior and the theoretical relation: together they provide a way to estimate hyperparameters in the large-network setting considered by the authors.

Simulation results compare the method with cross-validation and other techniques requiring matrix inversion. The authors report that their approach is efficient and precise in those comparisons. This supports response-based estimation as a promising computational alternative for the evaluated problems, with the reported evidence coming from simulations rather than a universal claim about every network or estimation task.
neurips-2001-fast-parameter-estimation-u.tldr: Empirically measured Green's functions support a hyperparameter-estimation method reported to be efficient and precise in large-network simulations.

paragraphs: Neural firing patterns contain information in both individual firing rates and relationships among neurons. This paper introduces an information-geometric measure for studying those relationships, including interactions beyond pairs. Its central concern is to separate different contributions so that a change in firing rate is not confused with a change in correlation.

For two neurons, the authors show how to test whether pairwise correlation differs significantly between two periods. Their construction isolates the correlation term orthogonally to firing-rate terms. This separation matters because the comparison need not assume independent firing under the null hypothesis: it can address differences in correlation while allowing a non-independent reference case.

The same framework links neural firing to behavior through mutual information. It decomposes that information into contributions conveyed by mean firing rates and by coincident firing. The authors then extend the orthogonal decomposition to three neurons and to general populations. The result is a systematic way to distinguish rate-related information from information associated with coordinated activity.
neurips-2001-information-geometric-decom.tldr: An information-geometric decomposition separates firing-rate and interaction effects when testing neural correlations and relating activity to behavior.

paragraphs: This paper estimates human body pose from monocular images using a nonlinear supervised model called the Specialized Mappings Architecture. The model contains several forward mappings, each responsible for particular regions of the image-feature space, together with an inverse mapping. Its structure allows different parts of the input space to receive specialized treatment.

Each forward function converts image features into body-pose parameters within its assigned domain. Learning must determine both those domains and the functions operating on them. Inference presents a related challenge: the system must estimate pose from an input while incorporating knowledge supplied by the inverse function. The architecture therefore couples specialization with reasoning in both mapping directions.

The authors address these problems using EM and alternating choices of conditional-independence assumptions. They evaluate the approach on synthetic and real video sequences of human motion. The stated contribution is an architecture and learning procedure for coordinating specialized pose estimators, with evaluation spanning generated and recorded motion sequences rather than a reported quantitative advantage in the abstract.
neurips-2001-learning-body-pose-via-spec.tldr: A supervised architecture learns specialized image-to-pose mappings and combines them with an inverse mapping for monocular body-pose estimation.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a general strategy for scaling learning algorithms to arbitrarily large datasets. Its reference point is the model an algorithm would learn from infinitely many examples. The practical question is how much data to use at each step while controlling the difference between a finite-data model and that idealized reference.

The strategy first upper-bounds that difference as a function of the numbers of examples used across learning steps. It then chooses those sample amounts by minimizing computational time subject to a probabilistic loss constraint. This makes data allocation part of the optimization problem: computational effort is chosen in relation to an explicit bound on model discrepancy.

The authors apply the framework to EM for Gaussian mixture models. Preliminary experiments on a series of large datasets provide evidence of its potential. The title thus refers to approximating an infinite-data learning outcome with finite computation, with the method's usefulness tied to obtaining a suitable loss bound and using it to guide the allocation of examples.
neurips-2001-learning-from-infinite-data.tldr: The paper allocates training examples across learning steps to minimize runtime under a bound on discrepancy from an infinite-data model.

paragraphs: The paper studies matching two trees that have no designated root. It approaches the task by constructing an association graph that expresses possible correspondences between the trees. This changes the representation of the matching problem so that graph structure can be used to identify subtrees shared by the two inputs.

The key construction gives a one-to-one correspondence between maximal cliques in the association graph and maximal common subtrees. A maximal solution cannot simply be extended, although that does not by itself make it globally largest. The authors then use simple replicator dynamics from evolutionary game theory to search for solutions in this graph-based formulation.

Experiments cover hundreds of uniformly random trees. In those experiments, the dynamics always returned a globally optimal solution. This is a strong empirical result because the dynamics cannot escape local optima. The paper therefore combines a precise structural correspondence with encouraging optimization behavior, while its reported success on the tested trees does not establish a universal global-optimality guarantee.
neurips-2001-matching-free-trees-with-re.tldr: An association-graph formulation and replicator dynamics found globally optimal unrooted-tree matches in every reported random-tree experiment.

paragraphs: The paper builds on a connection between Bayesian belief propagation and the Bethe free energy from statistical physics. Earlier results related belief-propagation fixed points to extrema of that energy and provided an algorithm guaranteed to reach a local minimum. This work investigates what other decompositions of the energy can reveal.

The authors interpret the Bethe free energy through two information-theoretic tendencies: minimizing pairwise mutual information and maximizing marginal entropy. They call this interpretation MIME. It gives an account of the objective in terms of dependence between variables and uncertainty in individual variables, making the structure of the optimization more explicit.

From a spectrum of decompositions, the authors construct a family of free-energy functions and develop an algorithm for each one. Each algorithm is guaranteed to converge to a local minimum of its corresponding objective. Preliminary simulations agree with the theoretical development. The guarantee concerns local convergence, so the result supplies convergent optimization procedures without asserting that they always find a global optimum.
neurips-2001-mime-mutual-information-min.tldr: MIME interprets Bethe free energy through information measures and derives a family of algorithms guaranteed to converge to local minima.

paragraphs: The paper begins with a direct goal for classification: increase the probability that future observations receive the correct label. It translates that goal into an optimization problem. This makes future classification probability central to the mathematical formulation, linking the procedure used to construct the classifier with the performance quantity the authors want to control.

The resulting problem is solved using convex optimization methods. The authors also show how Mercer kernels can be incorporated to obtain nonlinear decision boundaries. That extension matters because it allows the proposed formulation to represent more than a straight separating boundary while retaining the connection to the underlying probability-based objective.

A central result is an explicit worst-case bound on the probability of misclassifying future data. Such a bound provides a conservative statement about error within the formulation, rather than a promise of error-free predictions. The contribution combines a direct probabilistic objective, a convex optimization approach, and a kernel extension with an explicit account of worst-case classification risk.
neurips-2001-minimax-probability-machine.tldr: The minimax probability machine uses convex optimization to construct classifiers with an explicit worst-case bound on future misclassification.

paragraphs: Probabilistic mixture models can summarize data for clustering, classification, and prediction. With a continuing stream of observations, such a model could be updated repeatedly to follow the incoming distribution. The paper focuses on business settings where the model itself is a compact summary and frequent changes to that summary are undesirable.

In this setting, the central task is to monitor whether the existing model remains applicable. The authors formulate change detection as identifying when a mixture model no longer adequately represents incoming data. This places attention on the continued validity of a retained model, providing a basis for deciding when the observed population has changed enough to matter.

The paper proposes a principled solution and presents empirical results on synthetic and real-life datasets. The supplied formulation starts with independent, identically distributed observations. Its practical contribution is to make model applicability an explicit monitoring problem, connecting distribution-change detection with the need to preserve useful, stable summaries of data as new observations arrive.
neurips-2001-model-based-population-trac.tldr: The paper monitors when a retained mixture model stops adequately representing incoming data, supporting distribution-change detection without continual model updates.

paragraphs: Least Squares Policy Iteration combines least-squares function approximation with policy iteration for reinforcement learning. Its motivation comes from least-squares temporal-difference learning, which uses experience efficiently for prediction. The paper seeks to carry that benefit into control, where the learner must improve its action choices rather than only evaluate behavior.

The authors identify two challenges: the lack of a straightforward control application for the earlier method and the strong influence of state-visitation frequencies on its approximations. LSPI addresses these issues through a model-free, fully off-policy approach. It can use or reuse experience gathered from any source, allowing learning to draw on observations collected outside the policy currently being improved.

The method is tested on several problems, including a bicycle simulator. In that example, it learns to guide the bicycle to a goal efficiently after observing a relatively small number of entirely random trials. The result illustrates the practical value of combining reusable experience with least-squares estimation in a procedure that improves a control policy.
neurips-2001-model-free-least-squares-po.tldr: LSPI combines least-squares estimation and policy iteration to learn control policies from reusable off-policy experience.

paragraphs: This paper trains mixture models to classify nonnegative data by directly optimizing a discriminative objective. The authors derive multiplicative update rules with a simple closed form. Like EM, the procedure guarantees monotonic improvement and requires no tuning parameters, but the improvement is directed toward the models' role as classifiers.

The method includes generalized iterative scaling for log-linear models as a special case. Its learning rate depends on the sparsity of the training data. To exploit that relationship, the authors use nonnegative matrix factorization to obtain sparse distributed representations. They report that this feature-selection step substantially accelerates learning and makes the method practical for large problems.

Experiments find that discriminatively trained mixture models classify much better than comparably sized models trained with EM. The comparison highlights the importance of the training objective even when model size is similar. The contribution therefore joins a directly classification-oriented learning rule with a representation strategy that improves the efficiency of applying that rule.
neurips-2001-multiplicative-updates-for-.tldr: Simple multiplicative updates directly train mixture-model classifiers, while sparse NMF representations accelerate learning and experiments show gains over EM training.

paragraphs: Policy-gradient reinforcement learning relies on estimating how policy changes affect performance. This paper studies two choices involved in those estimates: representing state-action values with function approximation and including a bias term in their estimation. The focus is the rate at which performance-gradient estimates converge, rather than only the form of the value representation.

The first theoretical result shows that linear function approximation can slow convergence relative to estimating the gradient without that approximation. The stated comparison depends on the number of basis functions. The second result shows that a nonzero bias term can improve convergence, with the stated relationship involving the number of possible actions. The supplied abstract has damaged formulas, so exact factors cannot be recovered from it.

Experiments show significant improvements in policy-gradient convergence when the theoretical findings are used. Together, the results show that approximation and bias choices can materially affect gradient estimation. In particular, the reported benefit of a nonzero bias term makes convergence behavior an important consideration when selecting how state-action values enter the learning procedure.
neurips-2001-rates-of-convergence-of-per.tldr: The paper shows that linear value approximation can slow policy-gradient convergence, while a nonzero bias term can improve it.

paragraphs: A probability distribution over image features is related to, but distinct from, a distribution over images. This paper introduces the g-factor to describe that relationship. The factor depends on the chosen features and lattice quantization, independently of the training images. It therefore captures an aspect of the representation that matters when learning image probabilities.

The authors study maximum-likelihood learning in homogeneous Markov random field models whose clique potentials correspond to feature histograms. Their analysis identifies when potentials for different features decouple. They also show that approximating the g-factor allows potentials to be calculated analytically, connecting a property of the feature representation to the computation of model parameters.

A further result links the approximation to generalized iterative scaling. The authors use that connection to improve their multinomial approximation and introduce Bethe-Kikuchi approximations to simplify the iterative-scaling procedure. Computer simulations support the analysis. The contribution is a framework that explains how feature-level distributions shape image-level learning and uses that explanation to develop parameter-computation methods.
neurips-2001-the-g-factor-relating-distr.tldr: The g-factor connects feature distributions to image distributions and supports analytical and iterative methods for learning image-model potentials.

paragraphs: The paper extends hidden Markov models to allow countably infinitely many hidden states. This provides a framework in which the set of possible states is not restricted to a fixed finite collection. The challenge is how to handle the corresponding infinite collection of transition parameters without explicitly estimating each one.

The authors use Dirichlet-process theory to integrate out those transition parameters implicitly. Three hyperparameters remain and can be learned from data. Together they define a hierarchical Dirichlet process capable of representing varied transition dynamics. This replaces the explicit infinite parameter collection with a probabilistic construction governed by a small number of learned quantities.

The hyperparameters control the dynamics' time scale, the sparsity of the state-transition matrix, and the expected number of distinct states in a finite sequence. The framework also naturally permits an infinite alphabet of emitted symbols, with possible words in English text offered as an example. Its contribution is a structured way to express unbounded state and symbol possibilities while retaining interpretable controls over finite observed sequences.
neurips-2001-the-infinite-hidden-markov-.tldr: Dirichlet processes extend hidden Markov models to infinitely many possible states while leaving three learnable hyperparameters governing transition behavior.

paragraphs: The paper connects jointree inference in belief networks with an algebraic approach based on multilinear functions. In that algebraic view, inference is performed by evaluating and differentiating a function representing the network. The main computational challenge becomes finding a compact representation of that function, making representation size central to the usefulness of the approach.

The authors show that mainstream jointree algorithms are special cases of this algebraic framework in a precise sense. This establishes a formal relationship between familiar inference procedures and operations on multilinear functions. It gives jointree calculations an interpretation through evaluation and differentiation, placing those algorithms within a broader account of probabilistic computation.

The paper uses this relationship to prove new properties of jointree algorithms and discusses practical and theoretical implications. Its stated contribution is the correspondence and the results derived from it. By connecting the two views, it makes the algebraic formulation relevant to understanding established inference methods, rather than leaving it as a separate way to describe belief networks.
neurips-2002-a-differential-semantics-fo.tldr: The paper shows that jointree inference is a special case of evaluating and differentiating multilinear functions, enabling new theoretical results.

paragraphs: The paper develops a trajectory-based representation for reinforcement learning policies and value functions. It is motivated by the goal of rapid learning without interference or the difficulties of high-dimensional representations. Policies and values are represented nonparametrically along trajectories, making paths through a task the organizing structure for the learned information.

The trajectories and their associated policies and values are updated as value estimates improve or the task model changes. This couples the representation to the current understanding of the task. A trajectory is therefore part of an evolving learning procedure, with its stored decisions and values revised as more accurate information becomes available.

The approach is applied to periodic tasks, including hopping and walking. These applications require handling discount factors and discontinuities in task dynamics, with function approximation used for values at discontinuities. The authors also describe extensions intended to improve robustness to modeling error and sensor noise. These contributions address concrete complications in trajectory-based control without establishing that the motivating challenges disappear in every task.
neurips-2002-nonparametric-representatio.tldr: A trajectory-based reinforcement-learning approach updates nonparametric policies and values along paths and is applied to hopping and walking.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether temporal coherence in natural image sequences can explain two properties associated with primary visual cortex. Temporal coherence favors outputs that remain consistent over time. The authors investigate two approaches and obtain receptive fields resembling those of simple cells, as well as pooling behavior resembling that of complex cells.

The first approach extracts receptive fields whose outputs are as temporally coherent as possible. The resulting fields are oriented, localized, and multiscale. This provides temporal coherence as an alternative to sparse coding for modeling the emergence of simple-cell-like receptive fields, showing that the reported structures can arise from a different learning principle.

The second approach uses a two-layer statistical generative model that includes both individual-cell temporal coherence and temporal dependencies between cells. Learning from natural data produces simple-cell-like fields and complex-cell-like pooling. Both layers are learned together from scratch without supervision. This is the stated advance over earlier statistical models that learned one layer while fixing others in advance: the model learns both kinds of organization within a single procedure.
neurips-2002-temporal-coherence-natural-.tldr: Temporal-coherence learning from natural image sequences produces simple-cell-like receptive fields and, in a jointly learned two-layer model, complex-cell-like pooling.
